238 Bayshore Drive
Cape Coral, FL · 2026

A family estate that commands Cape Coral's most prestigious riverfront address — where the Caloosahatchee becomes the living room, 188 feet of seawall becomes three distinct worlds, and Moroccan craftsmanship meets the Florida tropics at every turn.

Knight Family Estate · Design Vision · 2026

The Water's Edge

188 Feet of
Caloosahatchee

Nearly double the standard Bayshore lot water frontage. The trapezoid lot widens at the river — your most expansive, most private, most sun-drenched space is at the water. Three distinct zones, each with its own identity.

Seawall Programming — 188 Linear Feet
Beach Lounge 50 ft

Total Seawall · 188 ft · SW → NE
01
Zone 1 · SW Corner · 50 ft
Elevated Sand Terrace
Above-seawall-cap sand terrace — fully contained, zero environmental impact, no riverbed permits. Deep sand bed within a Moroccan-tiled travertine perimeter sitting 18–24 inches above the cap. Teak chaises, tiki umbrellas, outdoor shower with zellige tile surround, swim platform bolted to the seawall face. The southwest position captures peak afternoon sun and sits furthest from the neighbor. Unique on all of Bayshore Drive.
02
Zone 2 · Center · 90 ft
Captain's Walk + River Cabana
Full composite captain's walk the entire center zone. Two 20,000 lb boat lifts — center console and 40+ ft cruiser. Separate jet ski lift. River-level covered cabana with full bar, ceiling fans, TV — at water's eye level looking south down the Caloosahatchee. Zellige tile backsplash at the bar. Rattan and teak furnishings. Built-in uplighting on pilings. Where evenings happen.
03
Zone 3 · NE Corner · 48 ft
Open Storage + Fish Station
Northeast corner zone — paddleboard and kayak storage, dedicated fish cleaning station with water and drainage. Open-air, utility-focused. Pushed toward the neighbor side. Beauty faces the open river.
Design Language

Modern Tropical
Moroccan Soul

Clean structural lines and floor-to-ceiling glass of contemporary architecture — warmed by zellige tile, hand-carved cedar, weathered teak, rattan, and the geometric precision of Moroccan craft. Rustic texture against modern restraint.

Teal · Primary Caloosahatchee
Terra · Warmth Moroccan Clay
Gold · Accent Zellige Glaze
Charcoal · Base Burned Teak
Moroccan Elements
Zellige Tile Throughout
Hand-cut Moroccan zellige tile as feature moments — entry foyer floor, outdoor bar backsplash, pool waterline, master bath feature wall, outdoor shower surround. The irregular reflective surface catches Florida light unlike any manufactured tile. Geometric starburst and arabesque patterns at key thresholds.
Rustic Finish
Reclaimed Teak + Hand-Carved Cedar
Reclaimed teak for outdoor decking, dock surfaces, and interior feature walls. Hand-carved cedar ceiling panels in the great room and master suite — Moroccan geometric lattice (mashrabiya) pattern backlit for evening ambiance. Weathered texture against clean plaster walls and glass.
Modern Tropical
Living Walls + Tropical Canopy
Interior living walls flanking the river glass facade — custom planted with tropical species that thrive in Florida light. Exterior Royal Palm and Bismarck Palm framing that continues Bayshore Drive's language onto the property. Dense planting buffers on northeast side toward the neighbor.
Interior Program

Room by
Room

Every room placed for a purpose. Ground floor: master suite (22×28) and fitness room east wing, private den off the master wing, great room (20×24) and kitchen center, glass wine room adjacent to dining, greenhouse (14×22) northeast corner, 3-car garage north side, office and cigar lounge and media room west wing. Glass elevator runs all three floors, south-facing river view as you ride. Second floor: three guest suites (14×22 each) with full en suites. Rooftop: open-air solarium and fire feature. Water's edge: tiki bar, covered boat lift, fire bowls flanking the infinity pool, integrated spa at pool deck.

Ground Level · Primary Living
The River Great Room
The entire south face of the main living level is uninterrupted floor-to-ceiling impact glass — two stories, no columns, the Caloosahatchee as the artwork. A double-height volume that reads as the home's heartbeat. Zellige tile fireplace surround as the interior focal point opposite the glass wall. Hand-carved cedar ceiling panels with backlit mashrabiya lattice above the living volume. The room that makes guests put their drink down. At 20 × 24 ft it's generous without being a hotel lobby — every inch of it faces the river.

Ground Level · West Wing · Hardened Construction
The Media Room
The whole room is the shelter — built to NBC spec from the foundation up: poured concrete or CMU walls minimum 8 inches, continuous ceiling slab, no exterior windows, all penetrations sleeved and blast-valved. Two ways in: a commercial-grade blast door from the corridor (walnut-clad, looks like any other interior door) and a hidden panel from the cigar lounge. In daily use it's a private media room — 85"+ screen, deep sectional, wet bar, surround sound. The back wall is full-height dark walnut paneling — identical to the rest of the room. Press a specific panel section and it swings inward into the gun room. No handle, no seam, no hardware. A touch latch or magnetic push latch behind the panel face — press, the door pops open an inch, you pull it through. Inside: long gun racks both walls, pistol safes at eye level, biometric rifle safe, ammunition storage, brass cleaning workbench. The gun room access is two layers deep — blast door or hidden lounge panel to get into the media room, then the hidden panel press to reach the guns. The shelter provisions are built invisibly into the room: HEPA/NBC air filtration, 72-hour water storage behind the wall finish, food provisions behind millwork, dedicated battery bank, satellite comms.

Ground Floor · Central Core · All Three Levels
Floating Staircase + Glass Elevator
The vertical circulation core is the first dramatic interior moment when you enter — positioned in the central foyer between the great room and the main corridor, south-facing so you ascend toward the light. Cantilevered walnut treads on a single steel spine. Frameless tempered glass panel railings with a continuous brass handrail. Open risers. Warm amber LED strip lighting under each tread. Adjacent to the staircase, a residential glass elevator runs all three floors — positioned on the south-facing interior wall so you are looking at the Caloosahatchee as you ride. Frameless glass cab, brushed brass threshold and call buttons, minimal mechanical footprint. At this level it is expected. On a 3-level riverfront estate it is also the most beautiful 8 seconds of your day.

A 4 × 6 ft recessed bay built into the north wall of the garage — the future home of a household robot. Boston Dynamics, Figure, Tesla Optimus — humanoid home robots are 5–10 years away and you are planning for them now. The alcove costs almost nothing during construction: a 240V dedicated circuit, a hardwired ethernet port, a flush wall-mount dock rough-in, a flat epoxy floor section, and overhead LED task lighting. When the robot arrives, it plugs in, connects to the network, and has a home. Everything else in the house is already designed to accommodate it: 36" minimum doorways throughout the ground floor, zero thresholds between rooms, continuous level floor plane, whole-home hardwired network. The alcove is the dock. The house is the operating environment.

Outdoor Living

The Land as
Resort

0.45 acres wider at the water than the street. The outdoor living program takes full advantage of the trapezoid geometry — everything expands as you move toward the river.

01
Primary Water Feature
Zero-Edge River Pool + Fire Bowls
SW corner placement — maximum angular separation from the neighbor, maximum open western sky. Zero south edge creates the illusion the pool flows directly into the Caloosahatchee. Zellige tile waterline in a repeating geometric pattern. Twin fire bowls flank both ends of the infinity edge — the reflection of open flame off the pool surface at night with the river behind it is the defining image of the property. No other home on Bayshore has this configuration at this position.
02
Pool Deck · Social Wellness
Integrated Spa + Jacuzzi
Spa integrated into the pool deck near the fire bowls — the social one. Hot water, fire bowls on either side, the river behind. Moroccan-tiled surround, spillover waterfall into the pool below. Seats 6–8. The evening move for guests, family, or a quiet night. Hot/fire bowl pairing on one end, infinity edge drop on the other — the pool deck has two distinct moments at each terminus. The cold plunge stays private on the master terrace for daily personal use.
03
Stepped Grade
Travertine Terrace Cascade
Grade change from finished floor elevation to seawall cap becomes tiered travertine steps with built-in planting beds, Moroccan lantern uplighting, and sun lounger platforms at each level. From the river approaching by boat, the home cascades to the water in a series of lit terraces. The exterior by night is the photograph that circulates.
04
Water's Edge · Zone 2
Tiki Bar + Covered Boat Lift
River-level covered cabana with full bar, ceiling fans, TV — at water's eye level looking south down the Caloosahatchee. Zellige tile backsplash. Rattan and teak furnishings. Built-in uplighting on pilings. Adjacent: covered boat lift with metal roof, lighting, water, and electric. Two 20,000 lb boat lifts for center console and 40+ ft cruiser, separate jet ski lift. The tiki bar is where evenings happen. The covered lift protects the vessel without becoming a structure with living quarters — practical infrastructure built to match the estate aesthetic.
05
Rooftop · Third Level
Open-Air Solarium
Sparse by design — the view does the work. 24 × 30 ft open deck with a central fire feature, two intimate seating areas, and an outdoor shower. No kitchen, no bar requiring staff. Morning yoga, stargazing, sunset with two glasses of wine. The rooftop is a private moment, not an entertainment venue — the quiet counterpoint to everything happening below at the pool and tiki bar. Accessible via glass elevator or staircase.
06
Privacy Screening
Northeast Landscape Buffer
Dense Clusia, Sea Grape, and Royal Palm planting on the northeast side toward 242. Creates a visual and acoustic buffer from the neighbor. Combined with the home footprint pushed northeast, your primary outdoor living zones — pool, fire bowls, spa, tiki bar — are fully private from adjacent properties.
Architectural Moves

The Statements
That Matter

The home is visible from Bayshore Drive and from the Caloosahatchee. Design both facades as primary. The river elevation is what every boater photographs.

River Facade
Design the River Elevation as Primary
Every weekend boater, every dolphin tour, every vessel on the Caloosahatchee passes Bayshore Drive. Symmetrical river elevation, architectural lighting on seawall and terracing at night, illuminated water features. Zellige tile accent panels on the river facade visible from the water. When your home is lit from river to roofline at dusk — that photograph circulates Cape Coral permanently.
Interior Drama
Glass Wine Room
Full glass wall visible from the dining room — climate-controlled, cedar-lined, backlit, 300–400 bottle capacity. The wine room is a design element first, storage second. Warm amber LED behind each rack row. Guests notice it the moment they sit down at dinner. Rare on Bayshore, standard in Naples ultra-luxury. Immediately elevates the comp tier conversation with any appraiser or future buyer.
Vertical Circulation
River-View Glass Elevator
A residential glass elevator on the south-facing interior wall — you see the Caloosahatchee the entire ride between all three floors. Frameless glass cab, brushed brass threshold and call buttons. At a 3-level riverfront estate it is expected. Here it is also the most beautiful 8 seconds of your day. A structural and architectural statement tucked into the circulation core alongside the floating staircase.
Structural Move
Cantilevered Master Over Pool
Master suite extended as a cantilever over the pool deck — dramatic shade for swimmers below, floating-over-water sensation above. Reads as architecturally bold from the river. Combined with the zero-edge pool, creates a layered water-over-water visual that defines the home's signature image. No other home on Bayshore currently has this.
Street Presence
Moroccan Entry Portal
The front entry is a moment — arched Moroccan portal in hand-formed plaster, zellige tile surround, hand-forged iron doors. The arch motif is restrained — one statement gesture at the threshold, not throughout. Modern clean planes on either side. The contrast is the point. Arriving at 238 Bayshore should feel like nothing else on the street.
LDB Build Standard

Built to
Outlast

As the builder and the owner, you control this. Build above code everywhere. When the next Ian hits, this home is the reference point on Bayshore Drive — and that story sells itself.

Envelope
Icynene Spray Foam + CMU Fortress
Full Icynene spray foam envelope — thermal performance that cuts HVAC loads dramatically in the Florida climate. CMU or poured concrete on all exterior walls. Impact-rated everything — windows, doors, sliders. The building science story that post-Ian buyers pay a premium for. You can tell it authentically because you built it.
Energy
Solar + Whole-Home Battery
Rooftop solar array integrated flush into the roof plane — not rack-mounted, not an afterthought. Tesla Powerwall bank sized to run the home through a Category 4 event. Whole-home generator as tertiary backup. The home runs through a hurricane without a flicker. In Cape Coral post-Ian, this is not a luxury feature — it's a primary selling point.
Systems
Smart Home from Day One
Lutron lighting, Crestron or Control4 AV, automated hurricane shutters, pool chemistry monitoring, dock cameras, whole-home audio with outdoor zones extending to every seawall zone. Wire it during construction — not as a retrofit. At this price point, buyers expect a home that responds to them. Program it for the family first, value-add for the eventual buyer second.
Wind Engineering
Two-Story Structural Design
A two-story home on the Caloosahatchee sees significant wind loads — engineer the structural system from day one. CMU or poured concrete on all exterior walls, steel moment connections at key points, impact glass rated for 200 mph. Post-Ian, this is the story that sells the home when you're ready. Build it right once.
Acoustic Isolation
The East Wing Acoustic Spec
The master suite and fitness room share the east wing. Four construction details isolate them completely — floating floor, decoupled wall, acoustic door, treadmill pad. Early morning workouts don't reach the bedroom. The bathroom between the two rooms adds a natural 15–20 ft acoustic buffer as a fifth layer. Full spec in the acoustic section below.
East Wing · Construction Specification

Acoustic Isolation

The master suite and fitness room share a wall. Built correctly from the foundation up, a barbell dropped at 5am doesn't reach the bedroom. Four layers of isolation — floating floor, decoupled wall, acoustic door, treadmill pad — plus the bathroom buffer. Spec every detail at the design phase. Retrofitting acoustic isolation costs 5× more and never works as well.

01
Layer One · Fitness Room Floor
Floating Floor
A rubber isolation mat system under the finished floor decouples the fitness room slab from the structural slab beneath it. Weights dropped, barbell racked, treadmill running — the impact vibration stops at the floating layer and never enters the building structure. This is the single most important detail. Without it, every footfall transmits through the concrete directly to the master suite. With it, the slab is essentially invisible to impact noise.
Specification
Product: Regupol 6010 or equivalent rubber isolation mat system
Thickness: 10–15mm rubber layer under finished flooring
Coverage: Full fitness room footprint — edge to edge, no gaps at walls
Finish floor: Rubber sport tile over isolation mat — no rigid tile directly on mat
Cost: ~$3–5/SF — essentially invisible in a full build budget
Noise type addressed: Structure-borne impact — the hardest to solve after the fact
02
Layer Two · Shared Wall Construction
Decoupled Wall
The wall between the fitness room and the master bathroom uses a double stud system — two separate stud frames with an air gap between them, or resilient channel clips that decouple the drywall from the studs. The cavity is packed with Rockwool Safe'n'Sound acoustic mineral wool. This construction kills airborne sound — music, TV, weight plates clanking, voices. A standard single-stud wall with batt insulation gives you STC 35–40 (you can hear conversation through it). This spec gets you to STC 55–60. At STC 55 you hear essentially nothing.
Specification
Framing: Double stud — two separate 2×4 frames, 1" air gap between
Alternative: Single stud with resilient channel clips — slightly thinner, similar performance
Insulation: Rockwool Safe'n'Sound — full cavity, both stud bays
Drywall: Two layers 5/8" Type X each side — mass matters
STC rating: 55–62 achieved — conversation inaudible through wall
Noise type addressed: Airborne sound — music, TV, voice, equipment noise
03
Layer Three · Connecting Door
Acoustic Door
A perfectly isolated wall fails completely at a hollow core door. The connecting door between the fitness room and master bathroom must be a solid core door with an acoustic door sweep and compression seals on all four edges. The seal compresses when the door closes, eliminating the gap that would otherwise transmit sound. This is the most overlooked detail in acoustic construction and the most common failure point. Budget properly for it — a correct acoustic door with full perimeter seals runs $800–1,200 installed. A hollow core door with a rubber sweep undoes everything else.
Specification
Door core: Solid core — minimum 1.75" thickness, STC 34+ rated
Perimeter seals: Compression seals all four edges — head, jamb both sides, sill
Door sweep: Automatic acoustic sweep — drops on close, lifts on open
Frame: Solid wood frame — no hollow metal frame (transmits vibration)
Upgrade option: Double-door airlock vestibule — two doors, small gap between — essentially soundproof
Noise type addressed: The gap — flanking path that bypasses wall isolation
04
Layer Four · Equipment Isolation
Treadmill Pad
The treadmill motor produces a low-frequency mechanical vibration that even a floating floor doesn't fully absorb — the motor frequency can resonate through the isolation mat at certain speeds. A dedicated treadmill isolation pad under the machine adds a second decoupling layer specifically tuned to motor vibration. Simple, cheap, completely invisible. Drop it under the machine before first use. Same principle applies to any motorized equipment — elliptical, spin bike with a direct-drive motor.
Specification
Product: IncStores Thunder Lock or Vibrashield equipment mat
Thickness: 6–8mm dense rubber, high-density core
Placement: Under treadmill, elliptical, and any direct-drive motorized equipment
Cost: $200–400 per machine — lowest cost item in the entire spec
Not needed for: Free weights, cable machines, benches, pull-up rigs
Noise type addressed: Motor vibration — low frequency mechanical transmission
Layer Five · The Natural Buffer
The Bathroom Between
The master bathroom sits between the bedroom and the fitness room — a deliberate layout decision that adds 15–20 ft of mass, two additional walls, and an air volume between the pillow and the weights. This is the fifth acoustic layer and it costs nothing — it's a layout decision made at the design phase. Even without the other four layers, the bathroom buffer alone reduces noise transmission significantly. With all four layers plus the buffer, the bedroom is acoustically isolated from the fitness room at a level that exceeds most recording studio standards.
The Flow Path
Bedroom → acoustic door → Master Bathroom → acoustic door → Fitness Room

Two acoustic doors. Bathroom air volume between them. Four layers of construction isolation in the fitness room itself. The sound path from a dropped barbell to the bedroom crosses: floating floor → decoupled wall → bathroom air volume → second wall → bedroom. At each transition, the energy reduces by an order of magnitude.

Kitchen Garden

Why Screened · Why Detached
Beautiful outside.
Productive inside.
Zero bugs. Always.

Southwest Florida has year-round pest pressure — whiteflies, aphids, caterpillars, leaf miners. No hard freeze means the bugs never reset. Open raised beds require constant chemical management. The screened enclosure eliminates the problem entirely. No-see-um mesh blocks every insect while allowing full natural airflow and light. Plants grow cleaner and faster than open-air beds.

Detached keeps the home's impact envelope intact — no greenhouse glass compromising hurricane resistance. The kitchen door opens to a zellige tile path. Deborah walks 30 ft, enters through the Moroccan arch gate, harvests dinner. Kitchen to plate in under two minutes.

When the sun drops into the Caloosahatchee and the zellige tile catches the last light — every material choice, every room placement, every foot of that 188-foot seawall will have been worth exactly this moment.

Life Design Builders · Value Analysis

Pricing Logic

How this home gets priced — and why the standard $/SF metric understates the real value. Two thirds of the value is in the water program and outdoor living, not the walls.

The Appraisal Problem

Appraisers use a contributory value method — each feature is priced by what it adds over a comp without it. The problem: there is no comp for 188 feet of improved Caloosahatchee seawall with a 50 ft cruiser lift and tiki bar. Appraisers make large adjustments on thin data and land conservative. The appraisal will lag the real buyer price by 15–20%.

Why $/SF Is The Wrong Metric

The blended effective $/SF on a $6.8M sale is $1,436/SF — meaningless in isolation because $2.75M of the value lives in the water program, seawall footage, and outdoor living. The interior is $750/SF. The Caloosahatchee is priceless. Price the components separately, then add them up.

Appraisal vs. Buyer Price: The appraiser gets to ~$6.6M using contributory value on thin comps. The right buyer pays $7.0–7.8M because they're not buying SF — they're buying the only home on the Caloosahatchee with 188 feet of improved seawall, a 50 ft covered lift, a tiki bar at water level, and a cigar lounge with a hidden door. That buyer exists in a marina, a boat dealership, or a family office — not in the MLS comp database.

The move that protects everything: Don't build it to sell immediately. Live in it 2–3 years. Let the market find you. Sell when the right buyer appears on your timeline, not theirs. The only scenario where you lose money requires a direct hurricane hit, forced sale, and a frozen market simultaneously.

No contingency — unit rates reflect real market pricing with buffer already built in. All figures 2026 SWFL market.

Your Reference Point: Current Bayshore build — slab, block, beam, trusses, roof on 3,140 SF = $136,000 = $43.31/SF. This estimate uses that same cost basis for equivalent shell scope and applies market rates above that baseline for all premium items unique to this build.

Not Included: Land cost (238 Bayshore Drive), furniture + FF&E (rugs, chairs, art, appliances, accessories), window treatments, boat purchase, landscaping maintenance, financing costs, interest carry during construction.

Ground Floor · West Wing · Architect Specification

The Study

Two rooms. One wing. A private office and a gentleman's club cigar lounge at the western end of the ground floor — both river-facing, both with independent outdoor access to a private water terrace, connected by a hidden bookshelf door. The aesthetic language is gentleman's club throughout — a historically grounded interior style built on dark walnut paneling, tufted leather, aged brass hardware, Persian rugs, and low amber light. Darker and more atmospheric in the lounge. Sharper and more restrained in the office. The same DNA, calibrated for two entirely different states of mind.

Two Entries. One Room.
The media room has two ways in. The corridor entrance has a commercial-grade blast door — walnut-clad, looks like any other interior door, rated for blast overpressure and radiation. Daily use goes through here. The second entrance is a hidden panel behind the whiskey display in the cigar lounge — private access when you want to move between the two rooms without going through the corridor. The whole media room is the shelter. The safe room function is in the construction — poured concrete walls, NBC air filtration, 72-hour provisions — not in a separate room behind it.
Room 01 · The Office · Ground Floor West Wing
The Office
01
Gentleman's club lite — productive, sharp, river-oriented. The same family as the lounge next door but calibrated for daytime clarity. Paneling on the back wall and one side wall only; the river-facing wall is floor-to-ceiling impact glass. Morning light fills the room as the day begins. A private exterior door opens directly to the shared water terrace — no interior path required. The hidden bookshelf door on the shared wall connects to the lounge. When the workday ends, you pivot, pull the flush mount, and step through.
Walls & Paneling
Paneling Species
American Black Walnut — medium-dark stain, satin finish. Two walls only (back + side). Lighter than lounge to preserve morning clarity.
Panel Style
Raised stile-and-rail paneling, full height to ceiling. No cap rail — continuous floor to ceiling.
Accent Wall
Zellige tile feature wall behind desk position — geometric arabesque pattern in teal and gold. Moroccan anchor point.
Ceiling
Flat plaster — off-white. Coffered detail optional. Keeps room bright overhead.
Flooring
Primary Floor
Wide-plank American Black Walnut hardwood — 6" planks, natural oil finish, matte. Continuous species with lounge for visual flow.
Rug
Hand-knotted Turkish oushak — warm tan and ivory field with geometric border. Grounds the seating area without competing with the zellige wall.
Threshold
Brass saddle at exterior terrace door. Recessed mat well at entry from main corridor.
Lighting
Primary
Recessed downlights — 2700K warm white, fully dimmed. Trim in aged brass.
Task
Articulating brass desk lamp — library arm style. Warm focused beam.
Accent
In-shelf display lighting on built-ins — LED strip, warm white. Uplighting inside shelving bays.
Sconces
Pair of aged brass wall sconces flanking zellige accent wall. Candle-style bulb, exposed.
Millwork & Built-ins
Desk
Custom built-in walnut desk — floating, cantilevered from paneled back wall. Integrated cable management, leather pull-out writing surface.
Shelving
Full-height built-in shelving — open display bays with brass adjustable shelf pins. One bay contains the hidden door mechanism.
Hardware
All hardware in aged/antique brass — pulls, pins, hinges. Consistent throughout both rooms.
Seating & Furnishings
Desk Chair
Tan or camel full-grain leather executive chair. Lighter tone than lounge seating — separates the two rooms visually.
Guest Seating
Two cognac leather club chairs — tufted back, brass nail-head trim. Positioned facing desk for meetings.
Side Table
Brass and smoked glass occasional table between guest chairs.
Special Features
Hidden Door
Paneled wall section on shared wall — pivot mechanism, recessed brass flush pull. Opens into cigar lounge. No visible gap or hardware when closed.
HVAC
Dedicated zone — independently temperature controlled from main house. Mini-split concealed in ceiling, brass grille trim.
Acoustic
Acoustic batting behind paneling on shared wall with lounge. Sound separation between rooms.
Terrace Door
Impact-rated glass pivot door — direct access to private water terrace. Consistent with main house glazing spec.
Room 02 · The Cigar Lounge · Ground Floor West Wing
The Cigar Lounge
02
Full gentleman's club. Darker, heavier, and more atmospheric than the office next door — this is the room the day ends in. Whiskey and cigars are the only brief. Full-height dark walnut paneling on all four walls, coffered ceiling, oxblood and cognac tufted leather club chairs on a Persian rug over herringbone walnut hardwood. Mashrabiya carved screens on the river-facing wall filter the light and allow natural ventilation. Negative pressure exhaust system contains smoke entirely. The hidden bookshelf door on the shared wall is the only connection to the office — when it's closed, nobody in this room knows an office is on the other side.
Walls & Paneling
Paneling Species
American Black Walnut — dark espresso stain, satin finish. Full four walls, floor to ceiling. Heavier and darker than the office.
Panel Style
Raised stile-and-rail full-height paneling with integrated pilaster detail at corners. Coffered upper section above 9-ft line.
River Wall
Carved mashrabiya screens in aged walnut — geometric Islamic star pattern. Full height, floor to ceiling. Set proud of the glass plane behind, creating a double-layer river view. Ventilation and privacy in one element.
Ceiling
Coffered walnut ceiling — deep box coffers with plaster inset panels. Dark, intimate volume. Low ambient light target.
Flooring
Primary Floor
Wide-plank American Black Walnut — herringbone pattern, dark oil finish. Continuous species with office, herringbone pattern distinguishes the room.
Rug
Hand-knotted Persian rug — deep navy, burgundy, and gold field. Large format, anchors the seating group. Authentic antique or reproduction.
Threshold
Brass saddle at exterior terrace door. Hidden door threshold flush — no saddle, continuous walnut floor plane.
Lighting
Primary Pendants
Three Moroccan brass lantern pendants — hand-pierced brass, candlelight-warm LED filament. Hung at varying heights over seating group.
Sconces
Aged brass candle-style wall sconces between paneling pilasters. Warm exposed filament. Dimmer controlled.
Bar/Display Accent
In-shelf LED strip lighting — warm white, behind whiskey display glass. Backlit effect. Separate dimmer circuit.
Target Ambiance
2200K maximum. Full room on dimmer. No overhead fluorescent or bright zones. Candlelight-equivalent at full dim.
Millwork & Built-ins
Whiskey Display
Full-height built-in display cabinet — backlit open shelving above, closed storage below with brass hardware. Smoked glass panels on lower doors. Holds 40–60 bottles display.
Humidor Cabinet
Integrated within built-in millwork — cedar-lined interior, climate-controlled (65–70°F, 65–70% RH), glass door, brass handle. Approximate capacity 150–200 cigars.
Hidden Bookshelf Door
Full-height bookshelf on shared wall with office — styled as part of paneling system. Pivot mechanism, recessed brass flush pull on lounge side. Books and objects displayed normally when closed.
Hardware
All hardware aged/antique brass — consistent with office. Nail-head trim on upholstery in brass.
Seating & Furnishings
Primary Seating
Four tufted leather club chairs — two in oxblood, two in dark cognac. Deep button tufting, brass nail-head trim. Arranged around central table.
Central Table
Low round table — aged brass base, smoked glass or dark marble top. Cigar ashtray station integrated.
Side Console
Walnut and brass console table along one wall — tray for decanters, additional glassware storage below.
Special Features
Ventilation
Dedicated negative pressure exhaust system — room maintained at slight negative pressure relative to adjacent spaces. Inline exhaust fan with external discharge. Smoke fully contained. Separate from main HVAC.
Mashrabiya Screens
Custom carved walnut screens on river-facing wall — set 6" proud of glass plane. Geometric Islamic star pattern. Provide natural ventilation through louvered detail, river view filtered through pattern, privacy from exterior.
HVAC
Dedicated zone — independently temperature controlled. Mini-split concealed, brass grille trim. Cool and dry for cigar preservation.
Terrace Door
Impact-rated glass pivot door — direct access to private water terrace, shared with office. Positioned on river-facing wall adjacent to mashrabiya screens.
